target_customer: Patients with severe high-frequency hearing loss who no longer benefit from hearing aids but are not ready for a cochlear implant, reached via ENT surgeons
problem: Many people hear sound but cannot understand speech. Auricle is developing an extracochlear neurostimulation implant that preserves residual hearing.
business_model: Medical device, pre-clinical, intended implant sales after regulatory approval

founders.name: Francis Wong
founders.background_notes: YC page: UK-trained surgeon, Stanford Biodesign Fellowship.

founders.name: Jay Dhuldhoya
founders.background_notes: YC page: led R&D, quality and manufacturing projects at Element Science; Stanford Biodesign Innovation Fellowship.

technical_complexity.rationale: A novel implant needing neurostimulation hardware, surgical approach, human studies and FDA clearance; the YC page says two acute human studies were done but a full implant is still being developed.

defensibility.rationale: Trademarked 'Hear and Understand' and a novel extracochlear approach with clinical data raise barriers, though incumbents have far larger resources.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Incumbents have not copied the approach per sources found; a startup overview lists them as the dominant implant makers (undated).

market_need_then: The company says millions fail hearing aids but score under 60 percent on word recognition tests and are not ready for a cochlear implant. No dated 2021 market sizing source was found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Empathetic and cautious with repeated investigational-device disclaimers (company site).

branding.community_and_virality: None found; the name is shared with unrelated companies (a tinnitus device company and a headphone brand).

brand_strength.rationale: A fitting anatomical name with a trademarked tagline, but confusable with other Auricle companies and no press on the brand.

outcome_analysis: Auricle remains pre-clinical, supported by YC, Stanford ecosystem partners and NIH grants, with only about 500 thousand dollars of private funding reported by aggregators. Whether it is operating is uncertain because PitchBook shows it out of business while a 2024 NIH award shows activity. The technology risk and capital needs of implants are the central challenge.
notes: Private funding of about $500K (YC, Digilife, Fogarty Innovation, North South Ventures, StartX) appears only in aggregator listings, so it is not recorded as a round. A $35M July 2023 round with M12 on Extruct is unsupported and ignored. A 2021 Form D was reported but amount unverified. PitchBook lists Out of Business Nov 2024, conflicting with the 2024 NIH award. Competitors left empty: the only source listing them is an undated overview.
